Where the data came from. The search index holds {0} entries built from the codebook: some are a single question, some a question paired with one of its answer options, and some stand for a family of sibling questions that share a stem. A request is turned into one line of text and compared against every entry; the closest entry is the answer. Nothing in that comparison is a language model. The test set is {1} requests whose right answer is known, plus {2} more written deliberately about things the codebook does not ask about. Those {3} are {4} codebook entries described {5} different ways each, so every count out of {6} below counts requests rather than distinct targets: {7} of them are {8} attempts at the same entry, and {9} is how many entries were tested at all. The {10} were written by a language model that was shown the right answer's wording first, so every hit rate below is a best case and not a field estimate. The {11} absent requests are the only part of this evaluation that was held back from every choice made while building it. For {12} of those {13} entries the right answer is a family of sibling questions rather than one question, and landing on the family counts as right. What each number counts. Top of the list is how often the right entry came back first: {14} of {15}. Another {16} landed on the right subject but the wrong question, and those count as misses rather than partial credit. Has a match at all is how well the similarity score tells an answerable request from an absent one. Is the top match right is how well that same score tells a correct answer from a wrong one, which is a different and much harder question. Threshold is the score below which the system declines to answer instead of guessing.

strings.text: Each bar is one topic, and its length is how often search put the right codebook entry first for the requests about that topic. What a request is. A short description of something someone wants to measure, of the kind you would type into the box at the top of this page. Every request used here was written from a single codebook entry, and that entry is what counts as the right answer for it — so "first" means the entry the request was written from came back at the top of the list.{0} {1} n counts requests, not entries, so a bar at n={2} rests on one entry: the narrowest bars are the least evidence, however long they look. There are no requests at all on {3}, so those topics have no bar — how well search does there has never been measured, which is not the same as it doing well.

Why one score does those two jobs so differently. Each figure here is a middle-of-the-pack score: at least half the requests in its group scored at or below it, and the figure is itself one of the scores that occurred. It is deliberately not called a median — on an even-sized group it is the value just above the middle, not the average of the two. An absent request: nothing in the codebook is close, so the best match is weak — typically {0} against {1} for a request the codebook can answer. Those two barely overlap, which is the high area. Answerable but wrong: something IS close, it just is not the right entry — {2} when the top match is right against {3} when it is wrong, and those two lie on top of each other. The highest-scoring wrong answer is {4}, above the middling right one. The score measures how similar the best entry it found is to the request, not whether that entry is the one you meant — so a confidently wrong answer is indistinguishable from a confidently right one.
